questions.problem:
$\,$ If you don't set an alarm, then you will oversleep.

Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional statement above?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

- $A:$ You don't set an alarm.

- $B:$ You will oversleep.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A⇒B,$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬A∨B.
$$

The negation of $A$ can be written as

- $¬A:$ You set an alarm.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ You set an alarm, or you will oversleep.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

$\,$ Set an alarm, or you will oversleep.

choices.value: Don't set an alarm, and you won't oversleep.
Set an alarm, or you will oversleep.
Set an alarm, or you won't oversleep.
Either you do not set an alarm, or you will oversleep.
Either you do not set an alarm, or you won't oversleep.

answer_fields.correct_value: Set an alarm, or you will oversleep.

questions.problem: Simplify the statement $¬(R⇒¬S).$
questions.worked_solution:
The conditional statement $P⇒Q$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $¬P∨Q:$

So, in this case, we have the following equivalence:

$$
¬(R⇒¬S)≡¬(¬R∨¬S)
$$

Distributing the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law, we have

$$
¬(¬R∨¬S)≡¬(¬R)∧¬(¬S).
$$

Canceling out double negation, we reach

$$
R∧S.
$$

So the given statement is equivalent to $R∧S.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $P⇒Q≡¬P∨Q$
- $¬(P⇒Q)≡P∧¬Q$
- $¬(P⇒Q)≡P∨¬Q$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our statements:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $P⇒Q$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $¬P∨Q.$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. From part I, we have the following equivalence:

$$
P⇒Q≡¬P∨Q
$$

By negating this statement, we get

$$
¬(P⇒Q)≡¬(¬P∨Q).
$$

Distributing the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law, we have

$$
¬(¬P∨Q)≡¬(¬P)∧¬Q.
$$

Canceling out double negation, we reach

$$
P∧¬Q.
$$

So, $¬(P⇒Q)$ is equivalent to $P∧¬Q.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true.
I only
I and II only
II only
I and III only

answer_fields.correct_value: I and II only

canonical_examples.problem:
Which statement is logically equivalent to the following conditional statement?

$\qquad$ If you take an umbrella, then you will stay dry.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

- $A{:}$ You take an umbrella.

- $B{:}$ You will stay dry.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A \Rightarrow B,$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
\neg A \lor B.
$$

The negation of $A$ can be written as

- $\neg A{:}$ You do not take an umbrella.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

$\qquad$ You do not take an umbrella, or you will stay dry.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

$\qquad$ Either you do not take an umbrella, or you will stay dry.

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

- $A{:}$ Use sunscreen.

- $B{:}$ You will get sunburn.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A \lor B,$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
\neg A \Rightarrow B.
$$

The negation of $A$ can be written as

- $\neg A{:}$ You don't use sunscreen.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

$\qquad$ If you don't use sunscreen, then you will get sunburn.

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $X \Rightarrow 
eg Y \equiv 
eg (X \land Y)$

- $
eg \left(X \Rightarrow 
eg Yight)\equiv 
eg X \land Y$

- $
eg \left(X \Rightarrow 
eg Yight)\equiv X \land Y$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our statements:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $X \Rightarrow \neg Y$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $\neg X \lor \neg Y,$ which by De Morgan's law is equivalent to $\neg (X\land Y).$

- Statement III is true, while statement II is false. From part I, we have the following equivalence:

$$
X \Rightarrow \neg Y\equiv \neg (X\land Y)
$$

By negating this statement, we get

$$
\neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right) \equiv \neg \left(\neg (X\land Y)\right).
$$

Canceling out double negation, we reach

$$
X\land Y.
$$

So, $\neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right)$ is equivalent to $X \land Y.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Rewriting Conditional Statement Using the Associative, Commutative, and Absorption Laws
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that the conditional statement $A \Rightarrow \neg B$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $\lnot A \lor \neg B.$ So, we have

$$
\neg (A \Rightarrow \neg B) \lor A \equiv \neg (\neg A \lor \neg B) \lor A.
$$

Now, we can distribute the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law:

$$
\neg (\neg A \lor \neg B) \lor A \equiv ( \neg (\neg A) \land \neg (\neg B) ) \lor A
$$

Canceling out double negations, we reach

$$
( \neg (\neg A) \land \neg (\neg B) ) \lor A \equiv (A \land B) \lor A.
$$

Finally, by the absorption law, we have

$$
(A \land B) \lor A \equiv A.
$$

So the given statement is equivalent to $A.$
